catalog_quote: Stress is lexically contrastive in Istanbul Judeo-Spanish, e.g. pera /ˈpera/ ‘pear’, perro /ˈper̆o/ ‘dog’ vs. Perá /peˈra/ (name of a neighborhood), parás /paˈras/ ‘money’, pashá /paˈʃa/ ‘dear child’. Like in all Spanish varieties, stress may fall on any of the last three syllables of the word. There are, however, relatively few nominal forms with antepenultimate stress: lágrima /ˈlagrima/ ‘tear’, múzika /ˈmuzika/ ‘music’. Many nouns with antepenultimate stress in Mainstream Spanish, instead, in Istanbul Judeo-Spanish have final stress: pasharó /paʃaˈro/ ‘bird’, numeró /numeˈro/ ‘number’, guerfanó ‘orphan’, albondigás ‘meat balls’, cf. MSp pájaro, número, huérfano, albóndigas, cf. also arvolé ‘tree’(MSp árbol). ... The shift of the stress from antepenultimate to final position may have taken place under the influence of Turkish and, for cognate words, such as numeró, French. Antepenulti…
sweep_summary: ladi1251 (Ladino/Istanbul Judeo-Spanish, catalog_kind 'lexical' from Hualde & Şaul 2011 JIPA p. 104). this search of works with stress in the title produced a single title hit: Domínguez Caparrós 2009 'The metrics of Sephardic song' (John Benjamins, doi:10.1075/lfab.2.18dom). Its Crossref abstract shows it is about the versification of Sephardic songs (syllable counts, heterometry, stanza forms, rhyme) — prosody-but-not-word-stress; full text is closed (benjamins.com 403, OpenAlex is_oa=false), abstract only; silent on the catalog's classification; acquisition priority none. Supplementary API checks (Crossref bibliographic search 'Judeo-Spanish stress accent'; OpenAlex on the still-to-obtain Bradley 2021 chapter, closed) surfaced no open, first-hand statement of Judeo-Spanish word stress beyond the held Hualde & Şaul 2011, whose p. 104 'Stress' passage was re-located verbatim in the text file we hold. catalog's classification unchanged; no new stress statement was found. Metadata with.

tone.quote: Semi-spontaneous questions were elicited in a Discourse Completion Task and analyzed using a ToBI-like annotation of nuclear pitch accents and edge tones. The data show that bilingual speakers vary their question intonation depending on whether they speak BJS or BG. In BJS, YNQs typically end high, WHQs end low, and AQs end high on the first component and low on the second. ... Studies further show that BJS and BG share pitch accent and boundary tone inventories of declaratives [11, 12, 13].

tone.quote: Контур A (H* L-L%) се характеризира с висока тонална цел в рамките на ударената сричка (лѝ) с последващ рязък тонален спад. Контур B (L+H* !H-L%) представлява постепенно тонално покачване до края на ударената сричка, следвано от плавен, но отчетлив спад до края на обръщението. Контур C (L+H* !H-%) ... се състои от постепенно покачване до края на ударената сричка, следвано от лек спад и устойчиво плато на основната честота. Контур D (L+H* H-L%) е изграден от постепенно покачване, което достига своя връх едва в крайната (следударена) сричка, с последващ плавен спад.
tone.translation: Contour A (H* L-L%) is characterised by a high tonal target within the stressed syllable (li) followed by a sharp tonal fall. Contour B (L+H* !H-L%) is a gradual tonal rise to the end of the stressed syllable, followed by a smooth but distinct fall to the end of the vocative. Contour C (L+H* !H-%) ... consists of a gradual rise to the end of the stressed syllable, followed by a slight fall and a sustained plateau of the fundamental frequency. Contour D (L+H* H-L%) is built from a gradual rise that reaches its peak only in the final (post-tonic) syllable, with a subsequent smooth fall.

tone.quote: we systematically account for the phonetic characteristics of the contours and determine their tonal composition and meaning, thereby situating them within the intonation systems of Bulgarian Judeo‑Spanish and Bulgarian. It is shown that both languages use the same inventory of contours: (1) L+H* !H‑% (the so‑called “vocative chant”), (2) L+H* H‑L%, and (3) L+H* L‑%.

As for the distribution of pitch accents, our analysis revealed that the same repertoire of six pitch accents (L*, H*, H+L*, L*+H, L+<H*, L+H*), was used in each of the three data sets. ... the most frequent pattern in both JUSPA and BULG is penultimate stress, for both pre-nuclear and nuclear position. sources.quote: After briefly presenting the literary genre of Sephardic song (18th–20th centuries), we comment on its principal metrical characteristics, which concern syllabism, the stanza, and rhyme. [...] Some striking features of the meter of Sephardic songs are: the important presence of heterometry, the vitality of the dodecasyllable (a reinterpretation of the accentual verse of Juan de Mena ...) and the vigour of the octosílabo (the French heptasyllable).
sources.note: Nothing about word-stress placement. The abstract (the only part reachable: benjamins.com could not be reached by automated download, OpenAlex reports no open copy) describes verse metrics of Sephardic songs — syllable counts (dodecasyllable, octosyllable), heterometry, stanza forms (zéjel, Purim stanza) and rhyme — situated in the history of Spanish versification. Literary metrics, not phonology; the Glottolog noise_flag is correct.
